ANTI-VENOM SHORTAGE

By: Nicky Troll | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Unique Selling Point:
ACTION, HUMAN DRAMA, SCIENCE and EFFECTIVE GOVERNMENT AGENCY

Summary:
It’s been a long time coming. Post COVID antivenom production took a back seat. The South African Vaccine Producers (a sub-division of NHLS) is the sole manufacturer and exporter to most of Africa. It’s not just snake anti-venom that’s an issue, scorpion and spider anti-venom supplies are also running dry.

Further information:
WHY DO WE CARE?
People and Pets are dying due to government ineffectiveness. In recent months, a 10 year old boy in the Eastern Cape died after being bitten by a snake as well as an adult man in Limpopo also from a snake bite. Currently a 13 year old boy is undergoing surgery at Wilgers hospital following a serious bite and no anti-venom available to treat him timeously.

INSIDERS
We have access to former employees at the SAVP that will speak to the shortages. The SAVP claims it due to an upgrade of their facilities – but that’s not the case. They also claim there’s no shortage, yet when you try and buy anti-venom there’s no stock available. We can do a bit of a sting to poke a hole in their lies.

ACTION
We have visuals of snake removals and releases – filmed for a local series – the producers have agreed to give us visuals (I’ll get the release form signed ). And then we can accompany a snake remover for insight into the dangers and widespread occurrence of snakes, spiders and scorpions in SA. Nick Evans

SCIENCE
We’ll be able to film scenes of milking snakes for venom – with the CEO of the African Snakebite Institute.

WHY DO IT?
Visually interesting. Tiny undercover element. Government Department failing South Africans, regional impact across the continent.

CASE STUDY
Young Christiaan recovering after a Snouted Cobra bite. He was catching frogs in a shallow pond on their farm near Baltimore in Limpopo and grabbed what he thought was a frog or a terrapin but got bitten near the wrist and as he pulled his hand out of the water, saw a large banded Snouted Cobra briefly latched onto his arm.

Christiaan attended one of the African Snakebite Institute Snake Awareness courses and could positively identify the snake. The trip, from being bitten to getting to the hospital in Ellisras, took more than one hour. The correct first aid protocols were followed - no arterial tourniquet. He describes the bite as very painful but remained calm. As we often see with Snouted Cobra bites he had no obvious neurotoxic symptoms but swelling and discoloration at the site of the bite.

Christiaan was treated with SAVP Polyvalent antivenom (not sharing specifics) and developed blisters at the site of the bite. He was transferred to a Pretoria hospital for further treatment and is recovering well. He will be going in for plastic surgery and is expected to make a full recovery. Photograph shared with permission.

VET EXPERT – DR. DEAN DE KOCK
SCIENCE EXPERT – JOHAN MARAIS.

FINAL SCRIPT | ANTI-VENOM

VO 9:
OPENING - USE ONE OF THOSE NATURE SHOTS AS THE FIRST SHOT WITH A BIT OF AMBIENT SOUND BEFORE THE VO
Those closest to 12-year-old Christiaan Mahne will say he’s wired differently - from a young age fascinated by everything that crawls, slithers, or roams.

But what began as an ordinary afternoon exploring the family’s Balltimore farm, with his younger sisters late last year, ended in a heart-stopping nightmare.

CHRISTIAAN // I saw something. It was underneath the water. // I thought it was a frog. And when I grabbed it // I pulled up my arm like this, I saw the yellow and the black band of the snake.
MASA: What was going through your mind?
CHRISTIAAN: I started to pray, and I said, oh, no.
MASA: Oh No!
CHRISTIAAN: It burned quite a lot when it bit me at first /

VO 9: Christiaan had recently been on a snake awareness course and knew the emergency protocols. His parents rushed him to hospital, aware that anti-venom often meant the difference between life and death.

The 90-minute drive felt like an eternity. Initially Christiaan was given just two vials of anti-venom, but after his mom, Juanita insisted, he was eventually given three more.

JUANITA: // if you get too little anti-venom, the poison has a bigger effect // the more the anti-venom is given in the right dosage, the less the tissue damage is going to be. // the extra anti-venom is between losing your hand and not losing your hand.

VO 9: Snake bites are anything but rare in South Africa: There are an estimated 4,000 incidents every year. More than 600 bite victims end up in hospital, with about 60 of those needing anti-venom .

Sadly, not all victims survive. Recently, a 10-year-old died in the Eastern Cape and an adult in Limpopo.

NICK CAR SCENE
MASA: We're in KZN now. It is peak snakebite season. We’re, on our way to meet a snake rescuer, Nick Evans.

VO 9: Within moments of arriving, we’re on the move.

NICK: //Yah, we've already got a call, so we better get moving.

VO 9: We’re told a BIG snake has been spotted and the home owners, not wanting to take any chances, called for help. In peak season - Nick gets between 10-20 calls a day.

MASA: When you arrive, people must be so relieved.
NICK: They're relieved when I catch a snake.

SNAKE CATCH SCENE
NICK: Always keep calm, as calm as possible
MASA: Not me!
NICK: Snakes are really scared of people, so it's going to try and hide, and then it's going to try and look for an escape route,

NICK: There. It just there.
MASA: It's there. // What snake is that?
NICK: That is a black mamba.
MASA: that’s my cue to step back
NICK: // when a black mamba opens its mouth, that's a warning. That's to say, get away. I don't like you.
MASA: Okay. The warning has been heeded by me. I will stay away.
NICK: // Wait till the head is reversed back in the tongs

VO 9: I stand back while Nick secures the Mamb,a to safely remove it from the property.

NICK: Black mamba is a highly venomous, as you know, the reputation of being aggressive is is not true. But when a bite does happen, it's always very serious. And if it's a serious bite, quite a lot of anti-venom is needed.
MASA: Whooo! [sigh of relief]

VO 9: But getting anti-venom is not always guaranteed - there’s a severe shortage in South Africa, And as we are the sole manufacturers and exporter of polyvalent anti-venom for African snake species - the shortage is putting lives at risk, not just in the country but internationally.

Our investigation will reveal that there are a number of contributing factors….

Johan Marais runs the African Snakebite Institute – focused on snake research and awareness courses, he works up close to venomous snakes every day.

LINK: A warning in three different languages. But here we go.

VO 2: Here, there are close to 400 snakes - while not all snakes are venomous, a bite from one that is, requires very specific treatment and anti-venom is a crucial part of it.

JOHAN: The current forms of anti-venom have been, produced for probably more than 40 years as it is now.

VO 9: Locally, anti-venom is produced exclusively by the South African Vaccine Producers, or the SAVP. The process takes months. A tiny dose of snake venom is injected into a horse, triggering the production of antibodies. Those antibodies are harvested, purified, and turned into antivenom.

While the product is internationally renowned, it’s of no use if you can’t get it.

JOHAN: // The bottom line is We ‘re in the middle of the snakebite season and you battle to purchase anti-venom right now.

VO 2: Curious to see just how difficult it is to get stock, we called the SAVP to place an order.

CALL TO SAVP SCENE
SAVP: HEllo
MASA: I'm looking for anti-venom.
SAVP: We don't have stock at the moment. // We're busy renovating the facility, so we'll only have stock again in March. April.

JOHAN: Major hospitals still seem to have stock, both private and in state hospitals. But the smaller hospitals are the ones that don't have the stock, so it's not looking good. //

VO 9: “Not looking good” sums up the Mahne family’s experience in the moments immediately after Christiaan was bitten. Of the three hospitals they called - only one had stock.

JUANITA: // I phoned and they said to me, go to Lephalale – they have.

VO 9: Anti-venom can’t be used sparingly. Treating a venomous snake bite takes at least 6 -12 vials - and even then, complications can set in fast.

Hours after receiving his dose of anti-venom - Christiaan developed a severe infection.

Despite access to treatment, he spent four weeks in hospital, had multiple surgeries, intense courses of antibiotics and now, a skin graft. It’s been a brutal fight.

JUANITA: I think with the extra three vials of anti-venom we got, // saved my child's hand// //there is tissue damage, but it could have been much worse, had he gotten less.


VO 9: Johan shows us the species that bit Christiaan, a snouted cobra.

JOHAN: The venom of the snake is both neurotoxic and cytotoxic. The neurotoxins affect your breathing, which didn't happen in his case, but the cytotoxins did some tissue damage. //

LINK: The anti-venom shortage is not only affecting humans, but animals too. And vets. Well, they're struggling.

VO 9: Dr Dean de Kock is a senior vet.

DR DE KOCK: // if you don't have antivenom, these animals will not survive.

VO 9: At this 24 hour Animal Hospital alone, up to 80 pets are treated in peak snake bite season.

DR DE KOCK: // it's very sad when you could save a patient and you don't because of the lack of anti-venom//

VO 9: They’re now using an imported product from India which requires what’s known as a special use licence from the regulatory authority.

DR DE KOCK: // We just haven't found this one as effective. This is anecdotal. / we tend to use more of these.
MASA: And how pricey are they?
DR DE KOCK: This is, is about 2000 rand cost price. And with that SAVP about 2500 rand cost price.
MASA: But you use More of that.
DR DE KOCK: Correct. So for Puff adder you've got to use between 3 and 6, vials. But the SAVP we could use about 1 or 2 and get away with it.

UPSOUND JOHAN: What he’s going to do now is bite on the film…

VO 9: Could it be a shortage of ingredients, like the venom? Johan says that’s not the issue because venom extraction isn’t complex.

JOHAN MILKING SCENE
JOHAN: There's no shortage of venom. // It's the process of immunizing the horses, of extracting blood from the horses, removing the serum, purifying it, and then making that available.
MASA: And should it be a problem?
JOHAN: It isn't the process It's been doing it for a hundred years. It's not rocket science.

VO 9: Our investigation revealed that the production of anti-venom at the SAVP has come to a complete halt. For the last two months, the organisation hasn’t supplied a single vial – not to snake keepers, not to veterinary practices and not to medical facilities.

DR CLOTHILDE OLIPHANT is the Chief Operations Officer at the National Health Laboratory Service. The SAVP falls under her portfolio.

She tells our producer a delayed facility renovation last year, is behind the current shortage.

DR OLIPHANT: //It was expected that the stockpile that was developed would cover the the renovations period, but the delays were unforeseen. and toward the end of the renovation the stockpile became depleted.

VO 9: Ageing infrastructure and damage caused by power outages has seen production limping along since 2021. Add to that temporary skilled staff vacancies and procurement challenges - it’s been a crisis building for years.

DR OLIPHANT: These renovations were essential for the SAVP to retain its manufacturing license. So, it was partly to ensure that we meet good manufacturing practices and, and, comply with the standards and also to modernize and, improve on the infrastructure.
PRODUCER: Sounds great, but the reality is it was badly planned. We're in a situation where we do not have polyvalent anti-venom available in snakebite season.
DR OLIPHANT: We are acutely aware of the challenge that this, lack of supply, implies or the impact that it's having at the moment

VO 7: Dr Oliphant insists the SAVP is strengthening management and improving operational systems. The facility is set to restart operations this month, but new anti-venom isn’t expected until April – just as snake bite season wraps up.

JUANITA: I think the anti-venom should be available so wildly and freely because, I mean, we have we have a vehicle so that we can drive to a hospital that's 130km away from us and all. A lot of people don't have that privilege


PROMOS

PROMO 1

VO: Razor-sharp fangs… lightning speed.

A bite from a venous snake could rapidly turn into a life threatening situation.

JOHAN: We ‘re in the middle of the snakebite season and you battle to purchase anti-venom.


PROMO 2

VO: Snakes are efficient predators. And without the anti-venom, a bite from a venomous snake could be fatal.

NICK: Black mamba is a highly venomous, // when a bite does happen, it's always very serious. And if it's a serious bite, quite a lot of anti-venom is needed.

VO: South Africa is all out of polyvalent anti-venom - right in the middle of snakebite season.


PROMO 3
VO: South Africa is in the midst of an anti-venom crisis. Supplies have run out at the hight of snake bite season. Leaving people and pets in life-threatening situations.

DR DE KOCK: // it's very sad when you could save a patient and you don't because of the lack of anti-venom//

And with that SAVP about 2500 rand cost price. MASA: But you use More of that. DR DE KOCK: Correct. So for Puff adder you've got to use between 3 and 6, vials. But the SAVP we could use about 1 or 2 and get away with it. UPSOUND JOHAN: What he’s going to do now is bite on the film… VO 9: Could it be a shortage of ingredients, like the venom? Johan says that’s not the issue because venom extraction isn’t complex. JOHAN MILKING SCENE JOHAN: There's no shortage of venom. // It's the process of immunizing the horses, of extracting blood from the horses, removing the serum, purifying it, and then making that available. MASA: And should it be a problem? JOHAN: It isn't the process It's been doing it for a hundred years. It's not rocket science. VO 9: Our investigation revealed that the production of anti-venom at the SAVP has come to a complete halt. For the last two months, the organisation hasn’t supplied a single vial – not to snake keepers, not to veterinary practices and not to medical facilities. DR CLOTHILDE OLIPHANT is the Chief Operations Officer at the National Health Laboratory Service. The SAVP falls under her portfolio. She tells our producer a delayed facility renovation last year, is behind the current shortage. DR OLIPHANT: //It was expected that the stockpile that was developed would cover the the renovations period, but the delays were unforeseen. and toward the end of the renovation the stockpile became depleted. VO 9: Ageing infrastructure and damage caused by power outages has seen production limping along since 2021. Add to that temporary skilled staff vacancies and procurement challenges - it’s been a crisis building for years. DR OLIPHANT: These renovations were essential for the SAVP to retain its manufacturing license. So, it was partly to ensure that we meet good manufacturing practices and, and, comply with the standards and also to modernize and, improve on the infrastructure. PRODUCER: Sounds great, but the reality is it was badly planned. We're in a situation where we do not have polyvalent anti-venom available in snakebite season. DR OLIPHANT: We are acutely aware of the challenge that this, lack of supply, implies or the impact that it's having at the moment VO 7: Dr Oliphant insists the SAVP is strengthening management and improving operational systems. JUANITA: I think the anti-venom should be available so wildly and freely because, I mean, we have we have a vehicle so that we can drive to a hospital that's 130km away from us and all. metadata.Unique Selling Point: ACTION, HUMAN DRAMA, SCIENCE and EFFECTIVE GOVERNMENT AGENCY
metadata.Summary: It’s been a long time coming. Post COVID antivenom production took a back seat. The South African Vaccine Producers (a sub-division of NHLS) is the sole manufacturer and exporter to most of Africa. It’s not just snake anti-venom that’s an issue, scorpion and spider anti-venom supplies are also running dry.
metadata.Further information: WHY DO WE CARE? People and Pets are dying due to government ineffectiveness. In recent months, a 10 year old boy in the Eastern Cape died after being bitten by a snake as well as an adult man in Limpopo also from a snake bite. Currently a 13 year old boy is undergoing surgery at Wilgers hospital following a serious bite and no anti-venom available to treat him timeously. INSIDERS We have access to former employees at the SAVP that will speak to the shortages. The SAVP claims it due to an upgrade of their facilities – but that’s not the case. They also claim there’s no shortage, yet when you try and buy anti-venom there’s no stock available. We can do a bit of a sting to poke a hole in their lies. ACTION We have visuals of snake removals and releases – filmed for a local series – the producers have agreed to give us visuals (I’ll get the release form signed ). And then we can accompany a snake remover for insight into the dangers and widespread occurrence of snakes, spiders and scorpions in SA. Nick Evans SCIENCE We’ll be able to film scenes of milking snakes for venom – with the CEO of the African Snakebite Institute. WHY DO IT? Visually interesting. Tiny undercover element. Government Department failing South Africans, regional impact across the continent. CASE STUDY Young Christiaan recovering after a Snouted Cobra bite. He was catching frogs in a shallow pond on their farm near Baltimore in Limpopo and grabbed what he thought was a frog or a terrapin but got bitten near the wrist and as he pulled his hand out of the water, saw a large banded Snouted Cobra briefly latched onto his arm. Christiaan attended one of the African Snakebite Institute Snake Awareness courses and could positively identify the snake. The trip, from being bitten to getting to the hospital in Ellisras, took more than one hour. The correct first aid protocols were followed - no arterial tourniquet. He describes the bite as very painful but remained calm. As we often see with Snouted Cobra bites he had no obvious neurotoxic symptoms but swelling and discoloration at the site of the bite. Christiaan was treated with SAVP Polyvalent antivenom (not sharing specifics) and developed blisters at the site of the bite. He was transferred to a Pretoria hospital for further treatment and is recovering well. He will be going in for plastic surgery and is expected to make a full recovery. Photograph shared with permission. VET EXPERT – DR. DEAN DE KOCK SCIENCE EXPERT – JOHAN MARAIS.
